_comment: Declarative vessel inventory for the substrate image. apply-inventory.sh reads this at boot (before systemd) to select which units run, so one image runs any SUBSET: a full local substrate, a minimal hub (store+control+api+transport), or a compute-only spoke. DEFAULT (no ENABLED_ROLES/ENABLED_VESSELS env) = every unit enabled, identical to today. Selection env: ENABLED_ROLES=comma,roles | ENABLED_VESSELS=comma,units (explicit, overrides roles) | DISABLED_VESSELS=comma,units (always off). Per-vessel fork remotes: repo_owner_default (or per-vessel repo_owner) + the `repo` field feed setup-git-push.sh / clone-vessel-repos so a fork can point vessels at its own GitHub org. NAMED PROFILE 'analysis-backend' (the minimum backend a white-labelled metabob-mcp client attaches to = discovery + concept-db + analysis-vessel + activity-api + store/identity/seed/infra deps) is not a role-group here because concept-db/analysis-vessel share the coarse 'compute' role; it is expressed as an explicit ENABLED_VESSELS list in scripts/substrate/deploy-analysis-backend.sh — keep that list in sync with the units below.
_profiles_comment: Named per-container rosters as EXPLICIT unit lists. Roles are coarse — 'compute' names goal-host, development, light-dispatch, boredom, analysis, ribosome, relevance-sink and local-tools together, so no role expression selects a subset of them. (The LLM resolvers used to be in that list too, which is why a spoke — whose whole premise is resolving models on its hub — enabled four local arms; they now carry role 'models', which 'spoke' excludes and 'hub'/'full' include.) That is why ui-only-up.sh had to bypass roles with a hand-written ENABLED_VESSELS list. A profile is that list, named and kept next to the units it selects. PROFILE=<name> wins over ENABLED_VESSELS and ENABLED_ROLES; DISABLED_VESSELS still subtracts afterwards. human-surface-vessel is deliberately absent from surface_node: it is a manifest vessel, which apply-inventory never selects or masks, and vessel-ctl installs it after readiness. CAVEAT (the reason a profile is not yet a guarantee): apply-inventory can only govern units this file names, so a shipped unit absent from `vessels` below runs regardless of the profile — that is how a UI-only box ends up running LLM resolvers. See the ungoverned-units warning apply-inventory emits at boot.

vessels._comment: Template seeding, split out of development-vessel's start phase so it cannot hold multi-user.target. Same role, so any selection that runs the vessel runs its seed — and any that masks the vessel masks the seed with it, which matters because the seed Requires= the vessel.

role=seed, NOT compute. It seeds templates once and exits (Restart=no), but its unit is deliberately Type=simple — declared oneshot, systemd holds multi-user.target until it EXITS, and the boot then sits behind ~98 template uploads (measured, and the unit file records it). substrate-ready classifies a resting unit as healthy on `role=seed OR Type=oneshot`; under role=compute this matched neither, so a unit that had logged 'Catalogue already populated — skipping seed' and deactivated successfully was reported `down`. That made substrate-doctor print FAILURES with all seven checks passing, and a readiness gate that fails on healthy units gets ignored — worse than no gate. seed is in every role group (hub/spoke/full), so this changes no topology.

Role 'models', not 'compute'. The four llm-* units SERVE models; everything else under compute CONSUMES them through discovery. Bundled together, no role expression could say 'run work here, resolve models on the hub' — which is precisely what a spoke is, so every spoke enabled its own arms and the arms ran wherever a provider key happened to be persisted. Still 'core': a substrate that serves models must have this answering, and substrate-ready reports a unit that is neither enabled nor active as SKIPPED rather than down, so a spoke without the models role stays green. This is the shared BASE resolver on its own port. The per-model arms are rendered at boot from llm-arms.json as llm-<id>, are not inventory-named, and are governed by the entrypoint's arm pass; the static llm-resolver-{google,haiku,opus} siblings that once sat here were deleted because they duplicated those arms on the same ports.

role=store, NOT compute: this vessel is After=surrealdb.service and writes impulse_relevance_metrics to SurrealDB directly (src/index.ts:19-38), unlike every other compute vessel which reaches its data through a resolver. Under role=compute it was selected by the spoke group, which includes compute and excludes store — so on a federated spoke it started, registered, reported healthy, and every write it made failed silently against a datastore that was not there.

The .service is the unit that actually runs the selection loop; the .timer above only pokes it. apply-inventory.sh masks by exact unit name, so listing only the .timer left boredom-vessel.service ungoverned by role selection — it ran on a hub whose role group excludes compute, where its only dispatch conduit (light-dispatch-vessel.service, compute, correctly masked) was absent. Every dispatch then failed to connect, and the connect-error path records a FAILURE OUTCOME per template, so infrastructure absence was written into the shared learning store as arm quality. Both units must carry the same role.

Below: 28 units that shipped in the image but were absent from this file, so apply-inventory could not disable them in ANY role — a UI-only container ran three LLM resolvers because of exactly this. Naming them here is what makes a role or profile mean something. Timer+service pairs list both: the service is what a stray `systemctl start` reaches.

Below: the .service half of timer-driven units whose .timer was already listed. Governed in EFFECT today (mask the timer and nothing schedules them), but not by name — so a stray `systemctl start <unit>` reaches a unit no role selected. Roles here are copied from each unit's own timer, never guessed, so a role that selects the timer selects the service with it.
